tasks.description: Use `ABC` and `@abstractmethod` to define an abstract `Shape` with an abstract `area()` method. Create a `Circle` that implements it.
tasks.hint:
`from abc import ABC, abstractmethod`
`class Shape(ABC): @abstractmethod def area(self): pass`
You cannot instantiate `Shape` directly — you MUST implement all abstract methods in subclasses.
tasks.walkthrough:
`Shape` declares `area` as abstract, so it promises nothing about how it works, only that it exists.
`Circle` provides a real implementation, which makes it a concrete class that can be instantiated.

tasks.description: Attempt to instantiate the abstract `Shape` class directly. Show that it raises a `TypeError`.
tasks.hint:
Try: `shape = Shape()` — Python raises `TypeError: Can't instantiate abstract class Shape with abstract method area`
This is intentional — abstract classes define an INTERFACE, not implementations.
Catch the TypeError and print a message.
tasks.walkthrough:
Python refuses to create an instance of a class with unimplemented abstract methods.
The TypeError message names the class and the missing method, which is caught and printed here.

tasks.description: Create a `Drawable` abstract class with abstract methods `draw()` and `resize(factor)`. Implement both in a `Square` subclass.
tasks.hint:
Multiple abstract methods: declare both with `@abstractmethod`.
A subclass must implement ALL abstract methods or it's still abstract.
`class Square(Drawable): def draw(self): ... def resize(self, factor): ...`
tasks.walkthrough:
Both methods are abstract, so `Square` has to implement both before it can be created.
Leave one out and the TypeError from the previous task appears for Square instead.

tasks.description: Define a `Protocol` class `Printable` with a `print_info()` method. Create a class that satisfies the protocol without explicitly inheriting.
tasks.hint:
`from typing import Protocol`
`class Printable(Protocol): def print_info(self) -> None: ...`
Any class with a matching `print_info()` method satisfies the protocol — NO inheritance needed!
This is called structural subtyping or 'duck typing' with type checking.
tasks.walkthrough:
`Book` never mentions `Printable`, yet it satisfies the protocol because it has a `print_info` method with the right shape.
`show` accepts anything Printable, and a type checker would confirm Book qualifies.

tasks.description: Compare abstract classes vs protocols: show a function that accepts any object with a `speak()` method, using Protocol for type hints.
tasks.hint:
`class Speaker(Protocol): def speak(self) -> str: ...`
`def make_noise(obj: Speaker): print(obj.speak())`
Any class with `speak()` works — Dog, Cat, Robot — without a common base class.
tasks.walkthrough:
Three unrelated classes share nothing except a `speak` method.
With an abstract class they'd all need to inherit from a common base. With a Protocol, the method alone is enough.

lesson.intro:
Sometimes you want to say "every Shape must have an area method" without
saying how each one calculates it. Abstract classes enforce that through
inheritance. Protocols do it without inheritance: anything with the right
methods counts. Both are about agreeing on an interface.

sections.heading: Abstract base classes
sections.body:
Inherit from `ABC` and mark methods with `@abstractmethod`. The class can't
be instantiated directly, and neither can a subclass until it implements
every abstract method. The base class describes the contract; subclasses
fulfil it.

sections.heading: What happens if you try anyway
sections.body:
Instantiating the abstract class, or a subclass that forgot a method, raises
a TypeError that names what's missing. That's the feature: the mistake shows
up at creation time, not later when the method is called.
sections.output: Can't instantiate abstract class Shape without an implementation for abstract method 'area'

sections.heading: Protocols: structural typing
sections.body:
A `Protocol` lists the methods something needs. Any class that has them
satisfies the protocol automatically, no inheritance required. This is
duck typing ("if it quacks like a duck") made explicit for type checkers.

sections.heading: Which to use
sections.body:
- Abstract class: you control all the subclasses and want shared code in the base.
- Protocol: you want to accept anything with the right shape, including classes you don't own.

In practice, Protocols are lighter and Python leans that way. Abstract
classes are still common in libraries and frameworks.

watch_out: Forgetting to inherit from `ABC`. Then `@abstractmethod` does nothing and the class can be instantiated.
A subclass with a typo in the method name is still abstract, because the real method wasn't implemented.
The `...` in a Protocol method body is literal; it's the ellipsis placeholder.
Protocols don't enforce anything at runtime by default. They're for type checkers and readers.
